title: Trump says US flight systems are 'ancient' but 'safe' after ground stop
html:
Watch: Trump calls US air traffic control system 'ancient' after flights grounded

  • Published

US President Donald Trump has said air traffic control systems that manage flights across the country are "ancient" and is pushing Congress to fund costly upgrades.

Trump called the systems "obsolete", saying they were at least "55 years old" and noted some towers were not in good shape structurally.

"It's very safe. But it's safe for a different reason because we do it very slowly," he said. "In other words, we travel slower. That's why you have lots of waits at the airport."

His remarks came a week after a historic ground stop halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials said the agency planned on Friday to share more information about what led to the four-hour ground stop on 13 November.

Top aviation officials within the Trump administration have previously said the cause was related to old equipment overloading, as well as updates to systems.

At a press briefing, Trump responded to some concerns about whether the ground stop issue was at all linked to other tech outages in the same week.

"They're all separate events," he said. "You know we have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen."

Trump says Congress "seems to be very receptive" to approving funds for air traffic system upgrade

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has explained a government contractor was upgrading an aviation telecommunications network, swapping out copper lines for fibre and installing a router, which directs traffic across the network.

The switch led the router to start flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. It is unclear whether the root cause of the issue was the wire replacement or a fault with the router.

As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced issues with voice and ground communications. It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.

More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled the day of the outage, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5mn passengers.

Ripple effects from the incident caused issues for days, with thousands more flights being cancelled or delayed over the weekend.

In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or return to gates.

The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.

Since the outage, transportation leaders have repeatedly pressed Congress for billions in funding to upgrade US systems and warned that without an overhaul outages like this would continue.

Trump on Friday weighed in and backed members of his administration, who are asking for $50bn (£38bn) to rebuild air traffic control systems. He said the transportation department had been allotted $12bn (£9bn), which is not enough for such a large undertaking.

"I said, 'Sean, let's not spend money to patch up all over the place because when we get the new system, everything's going to be torn out, so let's not spend the 12. Spend as little as you can to keep it going,'" Trump said he told Duffy, the transportation secretary.

He reiterated accusations that Congress - which is currently controlled by the Republican party - was blocking the funds.

"We need to have new air traffic control, and to do that we have to get the money now," Trump said.

"Congress has been very bad on it, but if there's any silver lining to what happened last week, it's that Congress seems to be very receptive now to giving us the money."
summary: Trump backed members of his administration who are asking for $50bn to rebuild air traffic control systems in the wake of last Friday's major outage.
